                                                       JUDGMENT

                          1.      By way of the instant Judgment, this Court shall dispose of both the
                          instant Petitions filed by the Petitioner, one being OMP No. 3/2026 filed
                          under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996
                          ["Arbitration Act"] for setting aside the Final Arbitral Award dated
                          17.07.2026 ["Impugned Award"] and the other being OMP (I) No.
                          10/2026, seeking restraining orders against the Respondent in respect of the
                          Subject Property being land in Khasra Nos. 518 (4-5) *less (2-16), 519 (0-

                          9), 520 (1-8) *less (1-3), 530 (3-5), 531 (2-3), 532 (4-16), 535/1 (1-4), 535/2
                          (1-4), and 536 (3-9), comprised in Village Gadaipur, Mehrauli, Delhi
                          ["Subject Property"], till the disposal of the Petition filed under Section 34.

                          2.      A brief factual background arising from the instant Petitions is stated
                          as under:

                                (i)    An Agreement to Sell dated 17.01.2022 ["ATS"] was executed
                                       between the parties herein, in relation to the Subject Propertyfor a
                                       total consideration of Rs. 22,00,00,000/- (Rupees Twenty-Two
                                       Crores only). As per Clause A of the ATS, the Respondent held
                                       title to the Subject Property in three distinct ways:

                                          (b) An undivided one-fifth (1/5th) co-ownership share in
                                              approximately 22 bigha 7 biswa spread across Khasra Nos.

                                              519, 516, 517, 518, 520 and 529, which is referred to as the
                                              "Co-Ownership Parcel"; and

                                          (c) An expectancy, dependent on the conclusion of pending
                                              family settlements to land comprised in Khasra No. 530, 531,
                                              532, 535/1, 535/2 and 536, then held in the name of, or under

                                       way of a cheque on the very same date that the ATS was executed.
                                       Subsequent payments of Rs. 1,00,00,000/- (Rupees One Crore

                                       Thousand only) were also made by the Petitioner on 21.01.2022
                                       and 27.01.2022, respectively.

                                       executed on 31.03.2022, which would have a direct bearing on the

                                       family settlement is not executed on or before 31.03.2022, then
                                       the Petitioner would be entitled to get a refund on the entire
                                       payment made by it at the rate of interest of 15% from the date of
                                       payment.In addition, Clause 7 of the ATS provided that if the

                                 (vi) In the interregnum, two registered Sale Deeds were executed in
                                       favor of the nominee of the Petitioner, M/s Ultraville LLP on
                                       28.07.2022 and 17.08.2022. Nine months thereafter, the Petitioner
                                       issued a Public Notice dated 15.06.2023 which was published in
                                       the „Times of India‟ newspaper, asserting his rights over the
                                       Subject Property.

                                (vii) On 03.08.2023, a meeting regarding the available land took place
                                       between the parties, through one Mr. Pradeep Singh.

                                (viii)Later on, the Deed of Exchange dated 03.05.2024 was executed
                                       between the Respondent and Smt. Neeta Anand, perfecting the
                                       former‟s title to the „Neeta Anand parcel‟ of the Subject Property.
                                       Upon gaining knowledge of this, the Petitioner immediately issued
                                       two Demand Letters dated 07.08.2024 and 31.08.2024, stating
                                       therein that he was ready and willing to proceed with the sale deed
                                       pertaining to the remaining land.

                                (ix) When the Petitioner did not receive replies to either of the
                                       Demand Letters dated 07.08.2024 and 31.08.2024 despite their
                                       due service upon the Respondent, he invoked the arbitration
                                       clause being Clauses No. 18 and 19 contained in the ATS by way
                                       of a Letter dated 26.10.2024.

                                (x) When no response was forthcoming from the Respondent, the
                                       Petitioner approached this Court on 06.12.2024 by way of a
                                       Petition under Section 11 of the Arbitration Act being ARB.P.
                                       2014/2024, seeking appointment of an arbitrator. Shortly
                                       thereafter, the Respondent terminated the ATS by way of a Letter
                                       dated 10.12.2024.

                                 (xi) Subsequently, vide the Order dated 10.01.2025, this Court
                                       appointed an arbitrator to adjudicate upon the disputes between
                                       the parties.

                          3.      After conducting an examination into the statements of claim and
                          defense, evidence and oral arguments on behalf of the parties, the Impugned
                          Award dated 17.07.2026 was passed by the learned Sole Arbitrator.
                          Operative portion of the Impugned Award reads as under:

                                          "XIII. AWARD

                                          144. In view of the foregoing analysis and findings, this
                                          Tribunal makes the following Award:

                                          (A) The Claimant's claim for specific performance of
                                          the Agreement to Sell dated 17.01.2022, in respect of
                                          the land more particularly described in the Statement
                                          of Claim, is hereby dismissed.

                                          (B) The Claimant's prayer for a declaration that the
                                          Notice of Termination dated 10.12.2024 is illegal, non
                                          est, null and void is declined as unnecessary, specific
                                          performance having been refused.

                                          (C) The Claimant's prayer for a permanent injunction
                                          restraining the Respondent from dealing with the
                                          subject property is declined as a consequential matter.

                                          (D) The Respondent shall refund to the Claimant the
                                          sum of Rs.97,00,000 (Rupees Ninety-Seven Lakhs
                                          only), this direction being made on the basis of the
                                          Respondent's own unconditional admission of record
                                          and not upon any counterclaim, none having been
                                          pleaded.

                                          (E) The Respondent shall pay interest on the said sum
                                          of Rs.97,00,000 at the rate of 15% per annum from

                                           17.08.2022 being the date on which the second of the
                                          two 2022 Sale Deeds was registered and the excess
                                          amount crystallized until the date of this Award. The
                                          Respondent ought to have refunded the excess payment
                                          in 2022 itself or at the latest upon termination of the
                                          contract; the contractual rate of 15% per annum under
                                          Clause 6 of the Agreement is applied by analogy.

                                          Taking the date of this Award as 17.07.2026, the period
                                          from 17.08.2022 is 3 years and 11 months. Simple
                                          interest at 15% per annum on the principal sum of
                                          Rs.97,00,000 for that period amounts to Rs.56,98,750
                                          (Rupees Fifty-Six Lakhs Ninety-Eight Thousand Seven
                                          Hundred and Fifty only), yielding a combined
                                          principal- and-interest sum of Rs.1,53,98,750 (Rupees
                                          One Crore Fifty-Three Lakhs Ninety-Eight Thousand
                                          Seven Hundred and Fifty only) as of the date of this
                                          Award.

                                          (F) In the event the total amount under (D) and (E)
                                          above is not paid within sixty days from the date of this
                                          Award, the Respondent shall be liable to pay future
                                          interest at the rate of 15% per annum on the
                                          outstanding balance from the expiry of that period until
                                          realisation.

                                          (G) The Respondent shall pay costs of Rs.25,00,000
                                          (Rupees Twenty-Five Lakhs only) to the Claimant. The
                                          Respondent held an admitted sum of Rs.97,00,000 from
                                          17.08.2022 and offered no justification for its non-
                                          refund either in 2022 or upon termination of the
                                          contract in December 2024. The Claimant was
                                          compelled to initiate arbitration proceedings to recover
                                          a sum the Respondent herself acknowledged was due.
                                          In these circumstances, a costs order in the Claimant's
                                          favour is just under Section 31A of the Arbitration and
                                          Conciliation Act, 1996. All other fees and expenses
                                          shall be borne equally by the parties.

                                           (H) All other reliefs claimed by either party and not

                          4.      It is pertinent to note that after the passing of the Impugned Award,
                          the Petitioner, seeking ad-interim reliefs, filed a Petition under Section 9 of
                          the Arbitration Act being O.M.P.(I) 10/2026 before this Court with the
                          following prayers:

                                          "(a) Pass an appropriate order restraining the
                                          Respondent, her agents, associates, employees, family
                                          members, etc., from encumbering, mortgaging, selling,
                                          dealing with, transferring possession, raising any
                                          construction, or otherwise creating any third-party
                                          interest in the subject property i.e. land in Khasra Nos.

                                          518 (4-5) *less (2-16), 519 (0-9), 520 (1-8) *less (1-3),
                                          530 (3-5), 531 (2-3), 532 (4-16), 535/1 (1-4), 535/2 (1-

                                          4), and 536 (3-9), comprised in Village Gadaipur,
                                          Mehrauli, Delhi, subject matter of the Agreement to
                                          Sell dated 17.01.2022, pending the filing, listing, and
                                          final disposal of the Petitioner's challenge under
                                          Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act,
                                          1996; and

                                                 Pass any other orders as this Hon'ble Court may
                                           deem fit and proper under the circumstances of the
                                           case."

                          5.      By way of this Judgment, O.M.P.(I) 10/2026 shall also be disposed of
                          by this Court.

                          6.      Learned Senior Counsel for the Petitioner contends that the Impugned
                          Award is in contravention with the fundamental policy of Indian law, is
                          patently illegal and as such, must be set aside. To substantiate his contention,
                          he submits as under:

                                 (i)    Finding of the learned Sole Arbitrator that the Petitioner failed to
                                       establish continuous readiness and willingness, is without
                                       consideration of the vital documentary evidence produced by the
                                       Petitioner and is, as such, perverse and vitiated by patent illegality.

                                (ii) Even after confining his analysis to only two of the Chartered
                                       Accountant Certificates and treating them as documents prepared
                                       for unrelated third-party regulatory purposes, the learned Sole
                                       Arbitrator gave a completely contrary finding to conclude that the
                                       Petitioner did not place on record any document evidencing
                                       availability of funds between 2022 and 2024. This is despite the
                                       Petitioner having produced the following documents:

                                          (a) Income Tax Returns for Assessment Years 2021-22 to
                                                   2024-25, reflecting income of up to Rs. 25.93 Crores;

                                          (b) Audit Reports;

                                          (c) Stock Valuation Reports showing liquid assets of up to
                                                   59.64 Crore capable of being liquidated at short notice;

                                          (d) Letter of the Federal Bank, certifying a subsisting account
                                                   balance of Rs. 13.95 Crore as on 09.03.2025; and

                                          (e) Chartered Accountant Certificates, which were general
                                                   net-worth certificates issued without any third-party lender
                                                   disclaimers.

                                (iii) It is submitted that the learned Sole Arbitrator ought to have
                                       considered the overall conduct of the parties, such as the payments
                                       made between 17.01.2022 and 17.08.2022, assistance in
                                       completion of the conveyances in the year 2022, immediate
                                       refutation of termination and pursuit of remedies under Sections 9,

                                        11 and 17 of the Arbitration Act, in conjunction with the financial
                                       record produced by the Petitioner. Reliance in this regard is placed
                                       on the judgment of the Apex Court in K.S. Manjunath v.
                                       Moorasavirappa, 2025 SCC OnLine SC 2378.

                                (iv) Finding of the learned Sole Arbitrator‟s that the Petitioner was
                                       required to maintain idle liquid funds exceeding Rs. 18 crores
                                       between 2022 and 2024 is unfounded on any legal principle
                                       whatsoever.

                                (v) The learned Sole Arbitrator has rendered mutually contradictory
                                       findings in the Impugned Award. It is submitted that the learned
                                       Sole Arbitrator first observed that the ATS depends on a single,
                                       indivisible contingency covering the entire Subject Property, and
                                       on the other hand,it observed that the Sale Deeds registered on
                                       28.07.2022 and 05.09.2022 constituted part-performance of the
                                       ATS and was not contrary to the terms of the ATS. The final
                                       findings in the Impugned Award, being based on such self-
                                       contradictory reasoning, cannot be sustained.

                                (vi) By construing that Clause 7 of the ATS contained a cut-off date
                                       (i.e., 31.03.2022) which was never agreed to between the parties,
                                       the learned Sole Arbitrator has rewritten the ATS and travelled
                                       beyond the jurisdiction conferred by the said ATS.

                                (vii) The learned Sole Arbitrator overlooked the crucial aspect that
                                       Clause 6 and Clause 7 of the ATS pertained to different family
                                       members of the Respondent, i.e., while Clause 6 relates to the
                                       immediate family members of the Respondent comprising her
                                       mother, sister and a family trust, Clause 7 relates to a relative of

                                        the Respondent, i.e., her aunt. Overlooking such an essential
                                       aspect goes to the root of the matter, and is not a matter of mere
                                       alternate interpretation, but one that was unreasonable, uncalled
                                       for and that frustrated the very intention of the parties while
                                       entering into the ATS.

                                (viii)The Respondent initially expressly mentioned in the Termination
                                       Notice that there was no objection to carry out the registry of the
                                       Neeta Anand Parcel. However later, the Respondent in the Section
                                       9 proceedings before this Court stated that since there was no
                                       agreement between the Respondent and Ms. Neeta Anand in terms
                                       of Clause 7 of the ATS, the same cannot be enforced, carefully
                                       concealing the factum of entering into the Deed of Exchange.The
                                       learned Sole Arbitrator ignored this dishonest conduct of the
                                       Respondent.

                                (ix) The Petitioner‟s readiness and willingness should have been
                                       assessed in light of the antecedent obligation resting upon the
                                       Respondent, who perfected her title to the Neeta Anand Parcel
                                       only on 03.05.2024 and thereafter, denied the very document
                                       through which the title was secured. However, the learned Sole
                                       Arbitrator, in violation of the judgment of the Apex Court in K.S.
                                       Manjunath (Supra), did not take into account the conduct of the
                                       parties.

                                (x) The Impugned Award violates the fundamental policy of Indian
                                       law by deciding the dispute on repealed equitable principles under
                                       former Section 20(2) of the SRA. By deciding on subjective
                                       notions of fairness and vendor hardship, the learned Sole

                                        Arbitrator acted ultra vires his jurisdiction and decided otherwise
                                       than in accordance with substantive law.

                                (xi) The learned Sole Arbitrator abandonedhis adjudicatory functions
                                       by refusing to decide upon certain framed Issues and by holding
                                       that the exact figure inserted in Clause 2 of the ATS does not need
                                       to be decided. It is submitted that leaving formally framed issues
                                       of contractual validity and agreed price unresolved while
                                       adjudicating consequential specific performance constitutes a
                                       manifest abdication of adjudicatory duty, giving rise to patent
                                       illegality on the face of the record.

                          7.      Per contra, learned Senior Counsel appearing for the Respondent
                          submits as under:

                                (i)    The learned Sole Arbitrator has correctly concluded that the time
                                       limit of 31.03.2022 stipulated in Clause 6 of the ATS was intended
                                       to be applicable to the land parcel mentioned in Clause 7 and not
                                       restricted to the land parcel in Clause 6 alone and consequently,
                                       the Respondent was discharged from her obligations under the
                                       ATS once the family settlement in relation to the Neeta Anand
                                       parcel did not fructify before 31.03.2022.

                                (ii) Interpretation of Clauses 6 and 7 of the ATS as given by the
                                       Petitioner would result in the Respondent being bound by the ATS
                                       for an indefinite period, which was not intended by the parties.

                                (iii) The learned Sole Arbitrator‟s interpretation of Clauses 6 and 7 of
                                       the ATS as well as the applicability of the deadline of 31.03.2022
                                       is a fair and reasonable interpretation of the contract out of which

                                        disputes have arisen between the parties, and as such, is least
                                       susceptible to challenge under Section 34 of the Arbitration Act.

                                (iv) By way of the present Petition, the Petitioner has only sought to
                                       reiterate an alternate plausible interpretation of the ATS which was
                                       also advanced before the learned Sole Arbitrator and struck down
                                       as untenable and unsupported by evidence. However, the
                                       Petitioner has not been able to show why the learned Sole
                                       Arbitrator‟s interpretation is untenable or implausible to warrant
                                       this Court‟s interference under Section 34 of the Arbitration Act.

                                (v) The Petitioner has been unable to identify as to which vital
                                       evidence was ignored by the learned Sole Arbitrator in arriving at
                                       the conclusion that the Petitioner was unwilling to execute the
                                       ATS.

                                (vi) Finding of the learned Sole Arbitrator on the Petitioner‟s financial
                                       capacity is one of facts and based on the relevant evidence
                                       produced by the parties and the Petitioner‟s objection on this
                                       count would call for re-appreciation of evidence, which is
                                       impermissible under Section 34 of the Arbitration Act.

                                (vii) The Petitioner‟s reliance on post-cut-off conveyances and
                                       payments to contend that the ATS did not terminate on the cut-off
                                       date is misconceived, and the learned Sole Arbitrator has correctly
                                       observed that the payment made on 12.04.2022 and other
                                       conveyances of the year 2022 relate to the Co-Ownership Parcel
                                       under Clause 6 and not Neeta Anand Parcel under Clause 7.

                                (viii)The Petitioner‟s contention that the SV Parcel fell outside the
                                       ambit of Clauses 6 and 7 of the ATS is fundamentally flawed as

                                        the ATS was entered into for the entire Subject Property, rather
                                       than for three (3) sets of separate parcels. As rightly observed by
                                       the learned Sole Arbitrator, this conclusion has been incorporated
                                       in Clause 7 of the ATS under the phrase "balance land out of
                                       approximately 5.50 acres."

                                (ix) It is submitted that the observations of the learned Sole Arbitrator
                                       on the Petitioner‟s readiness and willingness are factual, have been
                                       dealt with independently of each other and are based on
                                       appreciation of all the evidence produced by the parties. For
                                       instance, the observation of the learned Sole Arbitrator that the
                                       evidence did not depict readily deployable funds with the
                                       Petitioner between 2022 and 2024, was only arrived at after due
                                       consideration was given to the documents placed on record.

                                (x) In response to the Petitioner‟s contention that his ITRs for four
                                       assessment years was not looked into by the learned Sole
                                       Arbitrator, it is submitted that in the two relevant assessment
                                       years, i.e., 2023-24 and 2024-25, the Petitioner‟s income has been
                                       disclosed to be Rs. 4.09 crores and Rs. 9.91 crores respectively,
                                       which even cumulatively were in sufficient to fund the balance
                                       sale consideration of Rs. 18 crores. In any event, as rightly noted
                                       by the learned Sole Arbitrator, income tax returns are not
                                       sufficient to prove that funds were maintained in readily
                                       deployable form between 2022 and 2024 with the Petitioner.

                                (xi) The Petitioner‟s own audited balance sheet as on 31.03.2022
                                       shows a total of Rs. 1,89,59,44,118/- (approximately 189.59

                                       only Rs. 80,63,946/, as against the requirement of Rs. 18 crores.

                                (xii) The Chartered Accountant Certificates relied upon by the
                                       Petitioner to show financial readiness were issued specifically for
                                       the purpose of third-party lending institutions, in connection with
                                       regulatory and/or net-worth certification purposes. It is submitted
                                       that the Certificates expressly disclaim use for any other purpose
                                       and in any event, do not certify availability of funds for the
                                       transaction in question.

                                (xiii)The Petitioner‟s submission that the learned Sole Arbitrator has
                                       decided upon the merits of the case on equitable considerations is
                                       a plain misreading of the Impugned Award, as the learned Sole
                                       Arbitrator specifically notes that the statutory framework of SRA
                                       in respect if granting or refusing specific performance of a post-

                                       2018 contract prevents acting upon equitable considerations.
                                       Keeping this in mind, the learned Sole Arbitrator rightly identifies
                                       the operative bases of the Impugned Award as firstly, the lapse of
                                       the ATS on its stipulated temporal limit and secondly, the statutory
                                       bar under Section 16(c) of the SRA.

                          8.      Heard the learned Senior Counsels for the parties and perused the
                          material on record.

                          9.      Before deciding upon the rival contentions, this Court deems it fit to
                          remind itself of the contours within which the present Petition under Section
                          34 of the Arbitration Act must be adjudicated upon by this Court.

                          10.     It is trite law that a challenge to the arbitral award can only be on the
